2. If I rank w or y first, I have a higher chance of getting it due to my priority.
3. I should always rank my most preferred school first, unless there is a compelling reason not to.

Since x has the highest value ($62) and I have a priority of 2, I should consider ranking it first. However, I know that most applicants prefer y > x > w > z, so x is likely to be very competitive.

Let's think about dominated strategies. Suppose I rank z last. Is there any scenario where ranking z higher would be better? If I get rejected from my top three choices, ranking z higher might give me z instead of nothing. So, ranking z last is not necessarily dominated.

I need to balance value and priority. I have high priority at both w and y. Y has a higher value than w ($47 vs $42), so I should prefer y to w.

Consider ranking y first. If I get y, that's good. If I don't, I can then consider x or z. Since x has a higher value than z, I should rank x before z. Finally, w should be ranked last because it has the lowest value. This gives y > x > z > w.

Consider ranking x first. If I get x, that's great. If I don't, then I can consider y, z, and w. I should rank y before z and w. Then, I should rank z before w. This gives x > y > z > w.

Let's consider ranking z first. This is not a good idea because x has higher value and same priority.

Let's compare x > y > z > w and y > x > z > w.
If I can get x, then x > y > z > w is better.
If I can get y, then y > x > z > w is better.
If I cannot get x or y, then I will get z or w in both rankings.
Since x is the most valuable school, I should rank it first, even though my priority is only 2.
